'''''Eucalyptus cornuta''''', commonly known as '''yate''',<ref name=FloraBase>{{FloraBase|name=''Eucalyptus cornuta''|id=5605}}</ref> is a tree species, sometimes a [[Mallee (habit)|mallee]] and is [[endemism|endemic]] to the southwest of [[Western Australia]]. It has rough, fibrous bark on all or most of its trunk, smooth bark above, mostly lance-shaped adult leaves, elongated flower buds in groups of eleven or more, yellowish flowers and cylindrical to cup-shaped fruit. It is widely cultivated and produces one of the hardest and strongest timbers in the world.[[File:Eucalyptus cornuta buds(2).jpg|thumb|Flower buds]] [[File:Eucalyptus cornuta fruit(2).jpg|thumb|Fruit]] [[File:Eucalyptus cornuta trunk.jpg|thumb|Trunk bark]]

== Description ==
''Eucalyptus cornuta'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|25|m}} with a [[Crown (botany)|crown]] {{cvt|8-12|m}} wide, sometimes a mallee to {{cvt|10|m}}, and forms a [[lignotuber]]. New stems may fork out from the trunk or the lignotuber or multiple main stems may replace a single trunk in older specimens. It has rough, fibrous, brown to almost black bark on all or part of its trunk, smooth greyish bark above. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have egg-shaped to more or less round leaves {{cvt|40-70|mm}} long, {{cvt|20-70|mm}} wide and paler on the lower surface. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, the same glossy green on both sides, usually lance-shaped, mostly {{cvt|60-135|mm}} long and {{cvt|10-33|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|5-20|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in groups of eleven or more on a rounded to flattened, unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|12-32|mm}} long, the individual buds usually [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]]. Mature buds are elongated, {{cvt|23-42|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-8|mm}} wide with a horn-shaped [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] between four and seven times as long as the [[Hypanthium|floral cup]]. Flowering occurs between January and May or from July to November and the flowers are yellowish green. The fruit is a woody cylindrical to cup-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|5-12|mm}} long and {{cvt|6-13|mm}} wide with the seeds released through slits between the valves.<ref name="FloraBase" /><ref name=ps>{{cite web|url=http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au/Plants/Details/17851|title=''Eucalyptus cornuta'' Yate|access-date=21 December 2017|work=Plant Selector|publisher=Botanic Gardens of South Australia}}</ref><ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus cornuta'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_cornuta.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus cornuta'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20cornuta |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=14 May 2019}}</ref><ref name=Scott2013>{{cite book |last1=Scott |first1=Jane |last2=Negus |first2=Patricia (illustrator) |title=Wildflowers of Southwest Australia: Augusta-Margaret River Region |date=2013 |publisher=Cape to Cape Publishing |location=Fremantle |isbn=978-0-9803337-7-0 |page=149}}</ref><ref name="Lord1970">{{cite book |last1=Lord |first1=Ernest E. |author-link1=Ernest Lord |title=Shrubs and trees for Australian gardens |date=1970 |publisher=Lothian |location=Melbourne |isbn=0-85091-104-4 |page=34 |edition=4th |chapter=3. The Eucalypts (''Eucalyptus'')}}</ref><ref name=csiro>{{cite book|author1=Boland, Douglas J.|author2=McDonald, Maurice William|title=Forest Trees of Australia|date=2006|publisher=CSIRO Publishing|isbn=0-643-06969-0|page=334|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=q2v3kb9tFsYC&pg=PA334|access-date=24 January 2015|chapter=Yate}}</ref><ref name="Powell">{{cite web |title=Yate (''Eucalyptus cornuta'') |url=http://www.robertpowelltrees.org/yate-eucalyptus-cornuta/ |publisher=Robert Powell Tree Pictures |access-date=14 May 2019}}</ref>

== Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus cornuta'' was first formally described in 1800 by [[Jacques Labillardière]]. Labillardière collected the [[Type (biology)|type]] specimen from granite outcrops on [[Observatory Island]] west of [[Esperance, Western Australia|Esperance]] on 13 December 1792 during the [[Antoine Bruni d'Entrecasteaux|Bruni d'Entrecasteaux]] expedition. The description was published in his book ''[[Relation du Voyage à la Recherche de la Pérouse]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus cornuta''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/456056 |publisher=APNI|access-date=14 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="RSWA">{{cite journal |last1=Hopper |first1=Stephen D. |last2=Brown |first2=Andrew P. |last3=Marchant |first3=Neville G. |title=Plants of Western Australian granite outcrops |journal=Journal of the Royal Society of Western Australia |date=1997 |volume=80 |page=142 |url=https://www.rswa.org.au/publications/Journal/80(3)/80(3)hopper.pdf |access-date=14 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="Hopper2003">{{cite journal | first = Stephen | last = Hopper | author-link = Stephen Hopper | year = 2003 | title= South-western Australia, Cinderella of the world's temperate floristic regions 1 | journal = Curtis's Botanical Magazine | volume = 20 | issue = 2 | pages = 101–126 | doi = 10.1111/1467-8748.00379}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''cornuta'') is a [[Latin]] word meaning "horned" or "bearing horns",<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page=421}}</ref> referring to the operculum of the buds.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="Scott2013" />

The names in the [[Nyungar language]] of southwest Australia are ''mo'', ''yandil'', ''yeit'' or ''yate''.<ref name="Kipple">{{cite web|url=http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|title=Noongar names for plants|access-date=14 May 2019|publisher=kippleonline.net|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161120071826/http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|archive-date=20 November 2016}}</ref>

Yate is well established as a common name for this widely grown tree, and several other western species of eucalypt are so named: bushy yate ''[[Eucalyptus lehmannii|E. lehmannii]]'', flat topped yate ''[[Eucalyptus occidentalis|E. occidentalis]]'', river yate ''[[Eucalyptus macrandra|E. macrandra]]'', and warty yate ''[[Eucalyptus megacornuta|E. megacornuta]]''.<ref name="Wrigley">{{cite book |last1=Wrigley |first1=John W. |last2=Fagg |first2=Murray |title=Australian native plants: cultivation, use in landscaping and propagation |date=2003 |publisher=New Holland |location=Sydney |isbn=1-876334-90-8 |pages=540–42, 696 |edition=fifth}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Yate occurs in an area southeast of [[Busselton, Western Australia|Busselton]] to [[Cape Arid National Park|Cape Arid]] and the islands of the [[Recherche Archipelago]].<ref name="csiro" /> The species often occurs in isolated stands.<ref name="Scott2013" /> In more arid regions near Esperance, it is often at [[Granite outcrops of Western Australia|granite outcrops]], on deeper and wetter soil at cavities on the rock or the apron beneath the rockface.<ref name="RSWA" />
The species is found in a large mallee form at coastal areas, or as tall stands in areas of high rainfall and fertile soil of valleys, especially the inland region from [[Manjimup]] to the [[Porongurups]]. Vigorous early growth and the potential in its lignotuber allow it to generate new stems after fire or as new opportunities emerge in the canopy or surroundings. 
The form is similar to the [[mallee (habit)|mallee habit]] of smaller eucalypts in drier regions and its habit is comparable to limestone marlock, ''[[Eucalyptus decipiens|E. decipiens]]'', which occurs to the north and east. In favourable habitat a single trunk may attain great height and it is able to compete in tall forests of jarrah (''[[Eucalyptus marginata]]'') and marri (''[[Corymbia calophylla]]'') or any other species except the karri giants in ''[[Eucalyptus diversicolor]]'' forest.<ref name="Powell" />

==Uses==
===Use in horticulture===
The tree is sold commercially for use as an ornamental, shade or wildlife habitat. It will tolerate [[drought]], moderate [[frost]], a range of soils and in coastal areas.<ref name=ps/> While it may obtain great height in its natural habitat, the species is successfully planted as a medium or small tree for shade and [[windbreak]]s, and as street trees or for highway verges. Well known as a cultivated tree throughout Australia, ''E. cornuta'' has also been introduced to California.<ref name="Lord1970" /> [[Ferdinand von Mueller]] sent seed of the species to [[Lucknow]], where the sapling grew to a height of eight to ten feet within a year and, unlike eucalypts tested, tolerated tropical rain; his 1879 report also noted the successful introduction to [[Melbourne]].<ref name="Mueller1879">{{cite book |last1=Mueller |first1=Ferdinand |title=Report on the forest resources of Western Australia |date=1879 |publisher=Reeve |location=London |page=8 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/45214 |language=en}}</ref>

===Other uses===
This eucalypt produces one of the hardest and strongest timbers in the world and was formerly used for wheel spokes and the shafts of horse-drawn vehicles but most trees of commercial value were logged a long time ago.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="ABRS" /><ref name="C.A.Gardner">{{cite journal |last1=Gardner |first1=Charles A. |title=Trees of Western Australia. |journal=Journal of the Department of Agriculture  |series=Series 4 |date=1961 |volume=2 |issue=1 |page=93 |url=https://researchlibrary.agric.wa.gov.au/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?referer=https://www.google.com/&httpsredir=1&article=2505&context=journal_agriculture4 |access-date=14 May 2019}}</ref>
